svg.data-vd-play-label: Play: gas exchange across the alveolar wall
svg.data-vd-steps: [[0, "Ventilation brings fresh air into the alveolus, high in oxygen and low in carbon dioxide. Deoxygenated blood arrives from the pulmonary artery."], [2.5, "Oxygen dissolves in the moist lining and diffuses across the alveolar epithelium and the capillary endothelium (two thin, flattened cells) into the plasma, then into red blood cells, where it binds to haemoglobin."], [6.5, "Carbon dioxide diffuses the other way, from the plasma into the alveolus, down its own concentration gradient, and is breathed out."], [9.5, "Oxygenated blood leaves for the pulmonary vein. Constant blood flow and ventilation keep both concentration gradients steep, so diffusion stays fast."]]
svg.title: Alveoli and gas exchange
svg.desc: Left: a bronchiole ending in a cluster of alveoli covered by a capillary network, with a pulmonary artery branch bringing deoxygenated blood and a pulmonary vein branch taking oxygenated blood away. Right: a magnified section of the wall between two alveoli showing the moist lining, alveolar epithelium, basement membrane, capillary endothelium, plasma and red blood cells, with oxygen diffusing into the blood and carbon dioxide out.
svg.text: Left: alveoli at the end of a bronchiole. Right: the alveolar wall magnified (cell thicknesses exaggerated).

g.data-info: A narrow airway with smooth muscle in its wall (no cartilage) that carries air to and from the alveoli.
Tiny air sacs at the ends of the bronchioles: about 300 million in each pair of lungs, giving a gas exchange surface of roughly 70 m².
A dense network of capillaries covers every alveolus, giving a large blood supply that keeps the concentration gradients steep.
Carries deoxygenated blood (blue): a branch of the pulmonary artery brings it from the right ventricle to the alveoli.
Carries oxygenated blood (red): a branch of the pulmonary vein takes it back to the left atrium of the heart.
Air in the alveolus: high in oxygen and low in carbon dioxide compared with the blood arriving, because ventilation keeps replacing it.
A thin layer of water on the inner surface: gases dissolve in it before they diffuse. Surfactant lowers surface tension so the alveoli do not collapse.
A single layer of very thin, flattened (squamous) cells: part of a barrier only about 0.5 µm thick, so the diffusion distance is short.
A thin layer of protein fibres shared by the alveolar epithelium and the capillary endothelium.
The capillary wall: one layer of flattened cells, so oxygen and carbon dioxide cross only two thin cells.
The liquid part of the blood. It carries most carbon dioxide (as hydrogencarbonate ions) to the lungs.
The nucleus of a flattened epithelial or endothelial cell: the cell is thickest here, so the barrier is thinnest everywhere else.
Biconcave cells full of haemoglobin, squeezed in single file through the narrow capillary: close to the wall and slowed down, so they have time to load oxygen.

g.text: 1 Ventilation brings fresh air; deoxygenated blood arrives
2 Oxygen diffuses from the air into the blood and binds to haemoglobin
3 Carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveolus
4 Blood flow and ventilation keep both gradients steep
